531.quote_or_event: “Forgetting his Lord and Master, the mortal enjoys sensual pleasures; then, disease rises up in his body.”
531.explanation: In Raag Malaar Guru Nanak traces suffering back to pleasure pursued in forgetfulness of God.
531.tie_back: The Kural says the lapse that comes from excessive delight does more harm than unbounded anger; Guru Nanak shows the same sequence, indulgence breeding forgetfulness and forgetfulness breeding harm.
531.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1256, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
531._accuracy_note: Good fit on pleasure leading to heedlessness and ruin; Gurbani means forgetting God, not a ruler's practical carelessness, and makes no comparison with anger.

532.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, they do not forget the Naam from the mind; they are honored in the Court of the Lord.”
532.explanation: Guru Amar Das ties true honour to never letting the Name slip from the mind.
532.tie_back: The Kural says forgetfulness kills a man's good name; Guru Amar Das states the converse, that unbroken remembrance is what wins honour.
532.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
532._accuracy_note: Reasonable: the link between remembering and honour is shared, but the honour is in God's court rather than worldly fame, and the poverty simile is absent.

533.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, those who forget the Naam-what will happen when they go to the Court of the Lord?”
533.explanation: Guru Nanak asks what standing the forgetful can possibly have at the final reckoning.
533.tie_back: The Kural says the heedless never win lasting fame; Guru Nanak agrees that those who forget have no standing where it finally counts.
533.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 17, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
533._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the fate of the forgetful is shared, but Gurbani speaks of standing before God, not fame, and does not appeal to the agreement of all treatises.

534.quote_or_event: “Raawan made castles and fortresses of gold, but he had to abandon them when he left.”
534.explanation: Kabir points to the mythical king Ravana, whose golden fortresses could not hold him or save him.
534.tie_back: The Kural says no fortress helps the fearful and no advantage helps the heedless; Kabir likewise shows outer strongholds failing a ruler whose inner life had gone astray.
534.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1104, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
534._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the futility of fortresses is shared, but Kabir's point is death and transience, not fear or heedlessness.

535.quote_or_event: “If someone focuses on the Lord beforehand, then why should he be punished?”
535.explanation: In the Babarvani hymns on Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak says the suffering might have been avoided had people kept God in mind before the calamity struck.
535.tie_back: The Kural says one who fails to guard against trouble before it comes is left grieving afterwards; Guru Nanak asks why anyone would suffer if he had paid heed beforehand.
535.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
535._accuracy_note: Strong fit on foresight versus regret after the blow; the forethought Gurbani means is remembrance of God rather than military vigilance.

536.quote_or_event: “One who does not forget the Naam, for a moment or even an instant-how rare is such a person in this world!”
536.explanation: Guru Nanak praises remembrance that never lapses even for an instant, and notes how rare it is.
536.tie_back: The Kural says nothing equals watchfulness kept without a lapse towards everyone and at all times; Guru Nanak prizes the same never-lapsing attention, directed to the Name.
536.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 21, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
536._accuracy_note: Strong fit on unbroken attention at every moment; the object is God rather than the affairs of state.

537.explanation: In Sukhmani Guru Arjan lists the fruits of simran, among them that one's undertakings are brought to completion.
537.tie_back: The Kural says nothing is too hard for one who works carefully with an unforgetting mind as his tool; Guru Arjan says that remembrance brings one's works to completion.
537.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 263, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
537._accuracy_note: Good fit on remembrance accomplishing tasks, though Gurbani credits remembrance of God and divine grace rather than human vigilance as the instrument.

538.quote_or_event: “Meditate in remembrance on the Lord, or else you will regret it in the end, O mind.”
538.explanation: Kabir warns that neglecting remembrance now will bring regret when it is too late.
538.tie_back: The Kural says those who neglect the deeds the wise have praised will find no good in all their births; Kabir likewise warns that what is neglected now is lamented at the end.
538.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1106, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
538._accuracy_note: Partial: the warning against neglect is shared, but Kabir's essential duty is naam simran, not the royal duties of statecraft Parimelazhagar has in mind.

539.quote_or_event: “Many have proclaimed their sovereignty over millions of fortresses on the earth, but they have now departed.”
539.explanation: Guru Nanak calls to mind the many rulers who beat the drums of their power and are now gone.
539.tie_back: The Kural tells the one swelling with delight to remember those ruined by heedlessness; Guru Nanak recalls vanished rulers for the same sobering purpose.
539.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
539._accuracy_note: Reasonable: both use the memory of fallen rulers to check elation, but Guru Nanak's lesson is mortality and the vanity of power rather than heedlessness as such.

540.quote_or_event: “Meditate, meditate, meditate in remembrance of Him, and find peace.”
540.explanation: Sukhmani opens by urging repeated, unbroken remembrance as the way to peace.
540.tie_back: The Kural says what one has set the mind on is easily reached if one keeps thinking of it; Guru Arjan likewise makes sustained, repeated remembrance the means of reaching what is sought.
540.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
540._accuracy_note: Partial: sustained attention is shared, but the Kural's object is any chosen aim while Gurbani's is God and the fruit is inner peace.
